content: 1. A comprehensive list of all facility names, including key contact information such as addresses, phone numbers, distances from the point of entry, and route maps, must be created, maintained, updated, and disseminated. This information should be regularly tested for accuracy and accessibility to ensure it is available to all relevant personnel. These facilities are designated for the transfer of ill or suspected travelers from the point of entry. 2. Adequate staffing must be ensured, with access to a sufficient number of trained personnel assigned to these duties. The number of staff should correspond to the volume and frequency of travelers and the complexity of the point of entry, including terminal facilities, destinations, and multimodal practices. Arrangements for translation and interpreters should be made where necessary. 3. Competent and qualified personnel must be available for the prompt assessment, care, and reporting of ill travelers. These personnel should have undergone training programs to recognize disease symptoms and be familiar with procedures for prompt assessment, care, and reporting. 4. There must be adequate space to conduct private interviews with ill travelers. These spaces should be hygienic, environmentally safe, and appropriately sized based on the volume and type of travelers, as well as the complexity of the point of entry. Independent exit passages should be available for the safe transport of suspected travelers to medical care facilities to prevent the risk of infection to others. 5. Personnel conducting initial interviews and triage must use personal protective equipment (PPE). Access to appropriate equipment and trained personnel for the safe transport of ill travelers to medical facilities must be ensured. 6. Arrangements for the safe and hygienic transport of ill travelers to appropriate medical facilities must be in place. Transport service providers should have cleaning and disinfection equipment and supplies readily available. 7. Transport staff must have access to and use adequate personal protective equipment (PPE) when transporting ill travelers. The number of trained personnel should be sufficient to meet technical requirements for safe transport. 8. Personnel must be trained in standard operating procedures for the transport of ill travelers, including infection control techniques, the application of PPE, and the use of key information for contacting and accessing medical facilities safely and promptly. 9. Trained personnel must be available for the inspection of conveyances. The number of personnel should correspond to the volume and frequency of traffic, as well as the type, size, and kind of conveyances at the point of entry, to ensure timely and safe inspections. 10. Personnel must have demonstrable knowledge of required health-related documents for conveyances and their correct use for detecting, reporting, assessing, and implementing first control measures for public health events. 11. Personnel must be knowledgeable about the epidemiological situation at the point of entry, including common public health risks detected routinely and those associated with the type, size, and origin of conveyances using the point of entry. 12. Personnel must have the skills to detect, report, assess, and implement first control measures for public health events, including risks from microbiological, chemical, and radiological agents. They must understand how these agents affect human health and their modes of transmission. 13. Personnel must demonstrate knowledge of personal protective techniques and related equipment, including their correct application and use. 14. Personnel must have knowledge of public health measures, including disinfection, decontamination, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing, and entry/exit control. 15. Personnel must demonstrate knowledge of vector control methods for relevant vector-borne diseases, including disinsecting and deratting. 16. Personnel must have knowledge of safe food management practices, including handling, supply, sourcing, preparation, storage, and distribution. 17. Personnel must have knowledge of safe water management practices, including sourcing, storage, distribution, treatment, and control methods. 18. Personnel must have knowledge of solid and liquid waste management, including treatment, control methods, and systems for detecting, assessing, and implementing control measures for risks from waste, including bilge and ballast water for ships. 19. Personnel must have knowledge of risks associated with recreational swimming and spa areas, as well as methods and systems for detecting, assessing, and implementing control measures. 20. Procedures must be in place for monitoring human remains departing from and arriving at affected areas. These procedures should ensure safe handling and transport under the supervision of competent authorities, including the issuance of permits and proper sanitary treatment. 21. Facilities, equipment, and supplies for inspection staff must be available and maintained in safe and hygienic conditions. These include communication devices, testing and sampling supplies, updated guidance tools, PPE, vector control devices, and record-keeping systems. 22. An integrated vector control program must be in place, covering passenger terminals, cargo and container terminals, infrastructure, service provider facilities, and surrounding areas (minimum 400 meters from the point of entry). 23. Adequate numbers of trained personnel must be available to detect and control public health risks from vectors and reservoirs. These personnel should also oversee and audit services and facilities at the point of entry. 24. Monitoring of vectors and reservoirs within the point of entry and surrounding areas (at least 400 meters) must be maintained and updated. Detection, identification, pathogen testing, and control measures should be implemented, with audit results accessible. 25. Procedures must be in place for communication regarding suspected cases of communicable diseases or other public health events on board aircraft. These procedures should involve air traffic control, airport authorities, and public health sector authorities. 26. Procedures must be in place to assess, monitor, and safely apply aircraft disinsection and other vector control measures as required, following WHO recommendations and guidance. These procedures should be part of an integrated vector management control plan.
